label: Helly's Theorem
notes: Open the lecture by naming the compression principle. The students should hear Helly's theorem less as a combinatorial curiosity and more as a certificate theorem: when a finite convex intersection fails, the reason can be stored in at most d plus one constraints. This prepares them to read systems of inequalities through the same lens.

label: Classical Helly Statement
notes: State Helly in the forward direction, then immediately turn it around. In practice the contrapositive is the useful teaching form: if the full family is infeasible, the theorem promises a compact explanation. Emphasize that the number d plus one is the ambient affine dimension count, not the number of original constraints.

label: Intersection Problem
notes: Use this slide to separate the two verification modes. A feasible point is easy to audit because every constraint can be checked against the same vector. An infeasible family seems harder, because absence is global. Helly's theorem changes that by promising that, in finite-dimensional convex settings, absence has a bounded-size witness.

label: Planar Helly Picture
notes: Walk the audience through the two panels. On the left, the common point is a feasibility witness. On the right, the important feature is not the exact shape of each set, but the fact that convex boundaries create a genuine three-set gap. This is the first visual version of the d plus one certificate.

label: d+1 Certificate
notes: Frame d plus one as the storage budget for an infeasibility proof. The JSON asset is deliberately plain: it records the dimension, the named inequalities, and the arithmetic contradiction. This is the algorithmic side of the theorem, because a solver or a human can pass around the same small object as evidence.

label: Proof Dependency View
notes: Do not attempt to reproduce the long proof line by line. Instead, show the dependency pattern: a failed strict system is separated from an orthant, producing multipliers; weak systems require closedness and recession control; finite Helly is recovered by reducing to compact convex hulls of selected witness points. The common idea is always compression.

label: Systems Of Inequalities
notes: Connect the theorem language to the algebra students will actually manipulate. A convex inequality defines a convex level set, so solving a system is just intersecting those sets. The strict and weak versions matter, and affine equalities can be folded in as paired inequalities. This translation makes Helly immediately relevant to feasibility problems.

label: Infeasible Subsystem Certificate
notes: Present multipliers as proof objects. If the proposed feasible point existed, every strict inequality would make the weighted sum negative. The theorem supplies the opposite inequality everywhere on C, so both alternatives cannot hold. The drawing shows the finite half-plane version where the contradiction is simply f1 plus f2 plus f3 equals one.

label: Separation And Farkas Preview
notes: This is the bridge to the next section. The proof of the multiplier alternative separates a convex residual set from the nonpositive orthant. The separating normal becomes the vector of multipliers. In the linear case this pattern sharpens into Farkas-style alternatives and elementary-vector representation theory, which is why the section ends by pointing forward.

label: Example In R2
notes: Make the example concrete. The three inequalities say x is nonnegative, y is nonnegative, and their sum is at most negative one. Any pair can be satisfied, so pairwise tests are misleading. The three together sum to the contradiction one less than or equal to zero, exactly matching the planar Helly threshold.

label: Example In R3
notes: Use the three-dimensional example to show that d plus one is not cosmetic. The first three inequalities put the point in the nonpositive orthant, while the fourth demands a positive total sum. The four together are impossible, but dropping any one of them restores feasibility. This is the same certificate grammar in one higher dimension.

label: Numerical Helly Lab
notes: Translate the theorem into a computational workflow. The solver may search many subfamilies, but the returned object should be small: a named set J of at most d plus one constraints plus the arithmetic or geometric reason it is infeasible. This slide is also a warning that numerical success is not a proof until the certificate is independently verified.

label: Failure Outside Convexity
notes: This slide protects against a common overgeneralization. Pairwise intersection data can be arranged in a cycle with no common point when the sets are arbitrary. Convexity rules out that kind of disconnected bookkeeping by forcing segments between points to remain in the set. The theorem's power is exactly in that geometric structure.

label: Rule Ledger
notes: Treat this as the proof hygiene slide. Students should not merely remember a slogan about d plus one; they should identify which theorem is being invoked. Finite convex sets have the cleanest version. Infinite closed systems need recession control, and strict inequality alternatives need domain qualifications. The certificate is only valid after those hypotheses are named.

label: Recap
notes: Close by returning to the compression theme. The lecture should leave students with three moves: a point proves feasibility, a small subfamily proves finite convex infeasibility, and nonnegative multipliers prove inequality-system alternatives. The next section specializes to linear inequalities, where the same certificate logic becomes more algebraically refined.
